summary: Defines SNMP management objects for repeater devices based on IEEE 802.12, a local area network technology. Managers can use it to monitor and manage those repeaters.

eli5.summary: It gives managers a standard way to check on the equipment that repeats signals in one older kind of local network.

questions: how to manage 802.12 repeaters with snmp
what is the ieee 802.12 repeater mib
what is demand priority access method
subtitle: SNMP objects for watching and controlling IEEE 802.12 repeaters, the hubs of a 100 Mb/s demand-priority LAN.

tldr.problem: Network managers needed a standard way to monitor and configure repeaters for IEEE 802.12, a local area network technology that uses its own Demand Priority Access Method.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a MIB module, DOT12-RPTR-MIB, with tables for repeaters, port groups and ports, monitoring counters, address tracking and two notifications, closely following the counters and attributes of IEEE Standard 802.12-1995.
tldr.outcome: Repeaters that claim compliance implement the configuration, statistics, address-tracking and notification groups, so one SNMP manager can manage them uniformly.

today: RFC 2266 is a Proposed Standard published in January 1998. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose and the SNMP Framework
sections.content:
This memo defines part of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing repeaters based on IEEE 802.12 in TCP/IP networks. It is written with the SNMP Management Framework's Structure of Management Information, which describes objects with a subset of ASN.1. Each object type is named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, and an object type plus an instance identifies one specific piece of managed data.

The definitions follow Section 13, 'Layer management functions and services', and Annex C of IEEE Standard 802.12-1995. The counters are defined to be the same as the IEEE counters, so the same instrumentation can serve both the IEEE and IETF management standards. The IEEE document describes when and how each attribute is measured, in Pascal pseudocode.
sections.eli5: Every managed thing gets a name tag so a manager can ask for exactly the number it wants. This RFC makes the name tags for one kind of network relay.

sections.title: The Repeater Management Model
sections.content:
One managed system can contain one or more managed 802.12 repeaters and one or more repeater ports. The vgRptrBasicPortTable has an entry for each physical port. Implementors may group ports, for example one group per field-replaceable unit, so port numbering matches the hardware. This grouping is recommended but optional, and each port is identified by group number plus port number. Both may be sparsely numbered.

Repeaters themselves are rows in vgRptrInfoTable, identified by a repeater number. Each port is associated with one repeater or is isolated (a 'trivial' repeater). Ports of a single repeater share a contention domain and take part in the same instance of the Demand Priority Access Method. The column vgRptrPortRptrInfoIndex shows which repeater a port currently belongs to, and the mapping may be static or dynamic. Internal ports, such as a management port or a backplane connection, are also sources of traffic and may be placed in a group at the implementor's choice.
sections.eli5: A box can hold several relays, and each relay has numbered plugs. Plugs can be sorted into groups, like the cards in a rack, and each plug has a group number and its own number.

sections.title: Master and Slave Modes, Training and Framing
sections.content:
In an 802.12 network, 'master' devices act as network controllers and decide when requesting end nodes may transmit. A repeater acts as master on its local ports and as 'slave' on cascade ports that face an upper-level repeater. Devices that are not controllers, such as end nodes, are in slave mode.

When a link starts, the slave-mode device at the lower end sends training frames. Each has a destination address, source address, a 2-octet requested configuration, a 2-octet allowed configuration, 594 to 675 octets of data and a 4-octet frame check sequence. The destination address is always null. The master answers with an allowed configuration that can report a duplicate address, an incompatible configuration, or access refused for security reasons. Training completes only after 24 consecutive training frames are exchanged without error, which keeps marginal links from completing training.

A repeater can run in Ethernet or token ring framing mode. This changes only the frame format and address bit order, because 802.12 uses its own access method rather than either one. MAC addresses in the MIB are always in canonical order.
sections.eli5: Before two devices talk, they do a practice run. One asks for what it wants, the other says yes or no. They must practice 24 times in a row without a slip, so shaky cables fail the test.

sections.title: Structure of the MIB
sections.content:
Objects are arranged in OID subtrees, one per broad function. These subtrees are for organizational convenience only and have no relation to the conformance groups. There are three areas.

  • Basic definitions: status and control parameters for each repeater, port group and port.
  • Monitor definitions: statistics for each repeater and for individual ports.
  • Address tracking: the MAC addresses of the attached DTEs on each port.

Section 2.7 maps each IEEE 802.12 managed object (such as aPortAdministrativeState to vgRptrPortAdminStatus) onto its SNMP counterpart. Some IEEE objects were left out, for example the group and port maps, which a GetNext sweep of the tables can reveal. Octet counters come in a 32-bit form with a rollover counter, plus a 64-bit high-capacity form for systems that support Counter64.
sections.eli5: The MIB is a filing cabinet with three drawers: settings, scoreboards and a list of who is plugged in where.

sections.title: Relationship to Other MIBs
sections.content:
A repeater implementing this MIB is assumed to implement at least the MIB-II system group. Since the managed repeaters normally share one naming scope, there is usually one instance of the system group for the whole managed system.

The MIB-II interfaces group applies only to the interfaces the managing entity uses to send and receive management operations, not to repeater ports. An 802.12 repeater has an RMAC implementation but no DTE MAC, and it does not pass packets up to higher-level protocols.

Much of the existing IEEE 802.3 Repeater MIB does not apply, since it instruments the 802.3 access protocol. However, its separable snmpRptrGrpRptrAddrSearch group, which helps map network topology, is useful, and agent vendors are encouraged to implement it. The topology technology is patented by Hewlett-Packard, which granted rights to implementors of this MIB.
sections.eli5: This MIB does not replace the older forms. It plugs into them, and borrows one useful page from the form made for a different kind of network.

sections.title: Ports, Counters and Notifications
sections.content:
Port objects include vgRptrPortAdminStatus (enabled or disabled; enabling starts training on the link) and vgRptrPortOperStatus (active, inactive or training). The read-write vgRptrPortAllowedTrainType chooses what a port will accept: allowEndNodesOnly, allowPromiscuousEndNodes, allowEndNodesOrRepeaters or allowAnything.

Per-port statistics count frames and octets by kind, including readable, unreadable, high-priority and normal-priority traffic, plus broadcast, multicast, null-addressed, oversize and data-error frames.

Two notifications are defined. vgRptrHealth is sent when vgRptrInfoOperStatus changes, though not at power-up. vgRptrResetEvent is sent when a management-triggered reset completes, though not on agent restart. For each, the agent must leave at least a five-second gap between traps, and throttled traps are dropped, not queued.
sections.eli5: Each plug has a switch and a status light. Counters tally what passed through, and a repeater can ring a bell when its health changes, but not more than once every five seconds.

sections.title: Conformance
sections.content:
The compliance statement for managed 802.12 repeaters makes four groups mandatory: vgRptrConfigGroup, vgRptrStatsGroup, vgRptrAddrGroup and vgRptrNotificationsGroup. The vgRptrStats64Group is recommended for systems that can support Counter64.

Write access to vgRptrInfoDesiredFramingType is not required in a repeater that does not support configuring framing types. The snmpRptrGrpRptrAddrSearch group from the 802.3 Repeater MIB is recommended for systems that can search all incoming data streams for a particular source MAC address.
sections.eli5: A repeater that wants a gold star must support four required chapters of the MIB. Some extras are only suggested for devices that can handle them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Some of this management information may be sensitive, so SNMP requests should be authenticated and access controlled. How that is done is a function of the SNMP Administrative Framework and is not expanded by this MIB.

Several objects in vgRptrConfigGroup can be written, and setting them can seriously affect the network by changing the framing type, resetting the repeater, enabling or disabling ports, or changing the capabilities of attached end stations. Implementers are urged to require at least authentication of request origin for set operations.

The RFC singles out vgRptrPortAllowedTrainType as important for operational security. Administrators are advised to set it to allowEndNodesOnly on every port except those known to connect cascaded repeaters or devices needing promiscuous receive (bridges, switches, RMON probes). That stops unauthorized users from extending the network or listening promiscuously.
sections.eli5: Anyone who can change the settings can switch off the whole network, so only trusted people should be allowed to. One setting also acts like a door lock that keeps strangers from plugging in extra gear.

fields.name: DA
fields.desc: Destination address, six octets; always null in training frames.
